nameStory: Common gromwell gets its name from the Old French 'gromil,' meaning 'grain of millet,' referring to its hard, white seeds that look like tiny grains. The alternative name 'stoneseed' is even more descriptive – those seeds are so hard and smooth they truly feel like little white pebbles! European herbalists once ground these stone-like seeds into powder for medicinal use, which is why it's also called 'European stoneseed.'
description: Common gromwell is a medium-sized perennial herb that grows 1-3 feet tall with rough, hairy stems and leaves. It produces small, creamy-white flowers in clusters, but its most distinctive feature comes later – hard, shiny white seeds that look and feel like tiny stones. This European native has a somewhat weedy appearance with its coarse texture and upright growth habit. It's quite rare in New England, making any sighting special for plant enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: The plant's signature feature: hard, smooth, shiny white seeds about the size of small peppercorns that feel like polished pebbles when rolled between your fingers. They're produced in small clusters and persist long after flowers fade.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately on the stem, covered in stiff hairs that make them feel rough and sandpapery to the touch. The leaves have prominent parallel veins running from base to tip.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, creamy-white to pale yellow flowers about 1/4 inch across, clustered at the tops of stems. Each flower has 5 rounded petals and blooms from late spring through summer.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an upright perennial 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel rough and bristly. The whole plant has a coarse, somewhat weedy appearance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, angular stems covered in stiff, backward-pointing hairs that give them a distinctly rough texture – they'll catch on clothing when brushed against.

habitat: Common gromwell typically grows in disturbed soils, roadsides, old fields, and waste places, preferring well-drained, often rocky or gravelly ground. In New England, it's most likely to be found in areas with some human disturbance rather than deep woods. Look for it in sunny to partially shaded locations, often near old settlements or along transportation corridors.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with rough, hairy leaves. Look for the distinctive sandpapery texture of emerging foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with small white flowers in clusters. Seeds begin forming and hardening as summer progresses.
seasonality.fall: The characteristic hard, white stone-like seeds are fully mature and most easily spotted. Leaves may begin to yellow.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, but the persistent white seeds may still be visible among dried stems if you know where to look.

funFact: The seeds of common gromwell are so hard they can survive being eaten by birds and passing through their digestive systems completely intact – they're literally tough enough to be used as natural ball bearings! Medieval scribes actually used powdered gromwell seeds mixed with egg white as a durable white pigment for illuminated manuscripts.
confusionNotes: The rough, hairy leaves might remind you of other borage family plants like comfrey or borage itself, but those have much larger, more colorful flowers. Remember: if you find those distinctive hard white seeds that feel like tiny stones, you've got gromwell – no other common New England plant produces seeds quite like these.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'common' gromwell, it's actually quite rare in New England with only 11 recorded observations, making it an exciting find for botanists. This European introduction was once more widespread but has declined in recent decades, possibly due to changes in land use and agricultural practices.
compareHints: Common gromwell differs from its relative Virginia marbleseed by having white flowers (versus orange-yellow in Virginia marbleseed) and completely white seeds rather than mottled ones. Virginia marbleseed also tends to prefer shadier woodland edges, while common gromwell likes more open, disturbed sites. The stone-hard white seeds are the key feature that separates common gromwell from other borage family members.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relative common gromwell, Virginia marbleseed has much rougher, more sandpapery foliage and significantly larger, harder seeds that are truly marble-like.
